title: Very Learned, and Yet Making Little Show
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Meditations by Marcus Aurelius, in the Jeremy Collier translation.
body: Of Sextus, mildness and the pattern of a family governed with paternal affection; and a purpose to live according to nature: to be grave without affectation: to observe carefully the several dispositions of my friends, not to be offended with idiots, nor unseasonably to set upon those that are carried with the vulgar opinions, with the theorems, and tenets of philosophers: his conversation being an example how a man might accommodate himself to all men and companies; so that though his company were sweeter and more pleasing than any flatterer’s cogging and fawning; yet was it at the same time most respected and reverenced: who also had a proper happiness and faculty, rationally and methodically to find out, and set in order all necessary determinations and instructions for a man’s life. A man without ever the least appearance of anger, or any other passion; able at the same time most exactly to observe the Stoic Apathia, or unpassionateness, and yet to be most tender-hearted: ever of good credit; and yet almost without any noise, or rumour: very learned, and yet making little show.

From Alexander the Grammarian, to be un-reprovable myself, and not reproachfully to reprehend any man for a barbarism, or a solecism, or any false pronunciation, but dextrously by way of answer, or testimony, or confirmation of the same matter to utter it as it should have been spoken; or by some other such close and indirect admonition, handsomely and civilly to tell him of it.

Of Fronto, to how much envy and fraud and hypocrisy the state of a tyrannous king is subject unto, and how they who are commonly called nobly born, are in some sort incapable, or void of natural affection.

Of Alexander the Platonic, not often nor without great necessity to say, or to write to any man in a letter, that I am not at leisure; nor in this manner still to put off those duties, which we owe to our friends and acquaintances, under pretence of urgent affairs.

Of Catulus, not to contemn any friend’s expostulation, though unjust, but to strive to reduce him to his former disposition: freely and heartily to speak well of all my masters upon any occasion, as it is reported of Domitius, and Athenodotus: and to love my children with true affection.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the author learn from Sextus about living?
options: To live according to nature
To live for wealth and honor
To live in strict solitude
To live by the letter of the law

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what did Alexander the Grammarian teach the author to avoid doing?
options: Reproachfully correcting someone for a grammatical error
Speaking in public without notes
Writing long letters to friends
Arguing with philosophers

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did Fronto teach the author about kings?
options: How much envy, fraud, and hypocrisy a tyrannous king's position is subject to
How to rule wisely as a king
How kings should treat their soldiers
How to become a king oneself

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what phrase did Alexander the Platonic teach the author not to overuse in letters?
options: "I am not at leisure"
"I am deeply sorry"
"I demand an answer"
"I have no opinion"

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the author learn from Catulus about a friend's unjust complaint?
options: Not to dismiss it, but to try to restore the friend to his former disposition
To ignore it completely
To end the friendship at once
To report it to a third party

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the author praise Sextus for being "very learned, and yet making little show"?
options: True wisdom, in the author's view, doesn't need to be displayed to be genuine
Sextus was actually not very knowledgeable
Sextus was forbidden from teaching openly
Sextus preferred writing to speaking

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the author say the "nobly born" can be "void of natural affection"?
options: Fronto observed that the corrupting effects of power and privilege can hollow out ordinary human feeling
Noble families never had children of their own
Fronto believed only common people could love truly
Kings were legally forbidden from showing affection

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why did Alexander the Grammarian's method of correction work "handsomely and civilly"?
options: It corrected errors indirectly, without openly embarrassing the person
It relied on written notes rather than speech
It was performed only in private tutoring sessions
It involved rewarding correct speech with praise

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the overall point of the passage?
options: The author continues listing specific virtues he learned from different teachers and friends
The author argues that all his teachers were flawed
The author explains why he abandoned philosophy
The author describes a single dramatic event from his youth

questions.prompt: As used in the passage, what does it mean that Sextus achieved the Stoic "Apathia"?
options: A calm freedom from being ruled by passion or emotion
A total lack of interest in other people
An inability to feel physical pain
A refusal to ever change his opinions

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what did the author learn from Sextus about observing friends' dispositions?
options: To observe them carefully, without being offended by fools
To avoid friends who disagreed with him
To judge friends only by their wealth
To rely on others to judge his friends for him

questions.prompt: According to the passage, whose good example did Catulus cite for speaking well of one's masters?
options: Domitius and Athenodotus
Sextus and Fronto
Alexander the Grammarian and Alexander the Platonic
Rusticus and Apollonius

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what duties did Alexander the Platonic warn against neglecting?
options: Duties owed to friends and acquaintances
Duties owed to the state
Duties owed to one's teachers
Duties owed to strangers

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how did Sextus's company compare to a flatterer's?
options: It was sweeter and more pleasing, yet still respected and reverenced
It was harsher but more honest
It was identical in every way
It was less enjoyable but more useful

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the author value that Sextus was "of good credit... and yet almost without any noise, or rumour"?
options: It shows Sextus earned trust through character rather than seeking attention or fame
It shows Sextus was secretly dishonest
It shows Sextus avoided all public speaking
It shows Sextus was unknown outside his family

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what the author learned from Alexander the Grammarian?
options: How to correct others' errors gently and indirectly rather than through open criticism
How to write formal grammar textbooks
How to avoid speaking to uneducated people
How to memorize long passages of poetry

questions.prompt: As used in the passage, what does it mean to "contemn" a friend's unjust complaint, as Catulus advised against?
options: To treat it with scorn or disregard
To investigate it thoroughly
To agree with it immediately
To forget about it entirely
